title: Forms in React
intro: Forms are one of the most common places where React state, events, validation, and accessibility come together. In this lesson, you will learn how to build controlled forms, validate user input, handle submission, and give users useful feedback when something is wrong.
takeaways: Controlled inputs keep their current values in React state, while uncontrolled inputs let the DOM manage those values.
Text inputs use value and onChange, while controlled checkboxes use checked and event.target.checked.
Handle forms with onSubmit and preventDefault, then validate the data before processing the submission.
Touched state, aria-invalid, and aria-describedby help display validation feedback at the right time and make it accessible.
Client-side validation improves UX but never replaces backend validation because the backend must not trust data from the browser.

quiz.question: What makes an input a controlled React input?
options: It has a CSS class called controlled
Its value is managed through React state and updated with an event handler
It cannot be edited by the user
It is always an uncontrolled HTML input
quiz.explanation: A controlled input gets its current value from React state and uses an event handler such as onChange to update that state.

quiz.question: How should a controlled checkbox usually read its current value?
options: event.target.value
event.target.text
event.target.checked
event.target.selected
quiz.explanation: Checkboxes represent a boolean checked state, so controlled React checkboxes normally use checked and read event.target.checked.

quiz.question: Why is event.preventDefault() commonly used in a React form's onSubmit handler?
options: It prevents React from rendering
It prevents the browser's default form submission behaviour
It automatically validates every field
It clears all form state
quiz.explanation: preventDefault stops the browser's normal form submission behaviour, allowing the React application to handle the submission itself.

quiz.question: What does this validation expression check?
options: const validName = form.name.trim().length >= 2;
That the name contains exactly two words
That the name has at least two non-space characters
That the name contains two numbers
quiz.explanation: trim removes whitespace at the beginning and end, and length >= 2 requires at least two remaining characters.

quiz.question: Why should a Spring Boot backend validate data even if the React form already validates it?
options: React validation cannot be bypassed
Backend validation is only needed for styling
A client can bypass or modify browser-side validation and send requests directly
Spring Boot cannot receive data from React otherwise
quiz.explanation: Browser-side validation is controlled by the client and can be bypassed. The backend must validate incoming data independently before trusting or storing it.

exercise.title: Build a validated sign-up form
exercise.task: Create an `App` component containing a controlled sign-up form with a text input labelled `Name` using `id="name"`, an email input labelled `Email` using `id="email"` and `type="email"`, a checkbox labelled `I accept the terms` using `id="terms"`, and a submit button with the exact text `Sign up`. Keep the submit button disabled until the trimmed name has at least 2 characters, the email matches a practical `something@something.something` pattern, and the terms checkbox is checked. When the email contains a non-empty invalid value, show a paragraph with `id="email-error"`, `role="alert"`, and the exact text `Enter a valid email address`, and set `aria-invalid="true"` on the email input; the error should not appear for an untouched empty email field. On valid submit, call `preventDefault()` and replace the form with a paragraph using `data-testid="success"` that says exactly `Thanks, <trimmed name>!`. The tests use typeInto and click, so use real controlled inputs and a real submit button.
exercise.hint: Keep name, email, and terms in one state object, then derive validName, validEmail, and formIsValid from that state. Track whether the email has been blurred so an invalid non-empty email can show its accessible error. On submit, prevent the browser's default behaviour and use the trimmed name for the success message.

tests.name: renders the complete sign-up form
enables submit only when all fields are valid
valid name, email and terms enable submit
invalid email shows accessible error
successful submit replaces the form
